title: Trump says he will miss son’s wedding to stay in DC during ‘important time’
description_short: Trump says he will miss son’s wedding to stay in DC during ‘important time’
description_medium: Trump says he will miss son’s wedding to stay in DC during ‘important time’. US president previously said he would ‘try and make’ Donald Trump Jr’s nuptials but timing is ‘not good’ for him This entry is cataloged as a standalone event because it captures a concrete action, public statement, legal development, documented relationship, or policy consequence linked directly or indirectly to Trump. The downstream effects include institutional stress, public-trust erosion, and accountability pressure across affected systems.
description_long: Donald Trump said he would miss his eldest son Donald Trump Jr.’s wedding, after first telling reporters he would try to attend. The Guardian reported that the ceremony was expected in the Bahamas over Memorial Day weekend and quoted Trump’s explanation that government circumstances required him to remain in Washington. He also named the Iran war as a competing demand. In a Truth Social post, he offered congratulations to the couple and said he needed to stay at the White House during an important period. The report noted that Trump had recently attended sporting events and played golf, details that put his explanation in context but do not establish what specifically required his presence. The story records his public decision and stated rationale; it does not independently identify a scheduled government event or report whether his plans changed after publication.

title: Tulsi Gabbard Resigns as DNI Over Iran Conflict
description_short: Tulsi Gabbard Resigns as DNI Over Iran Conflict
description_medium: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard abruptly resigned from the administration following fierce internal disagreements with President Trump over military operations against Iran. Her departure marked the loss of another senior official during a critical geopolitical crisis, highlighting Trump's inability to maintain a stable national security team and his tendency to isolate dissenting voices even when the country is at war.
description_long: The Associated Press reported that Tulsi Gabbard resigned as director of national intelligence and cited her husband’s health as the reason. That account does not substantiate the supplied description’s claim that she left after a fierce dispute with Trump over Iran operations. The article’s headline and report frame the departure around her husband’s health; they do not provide evidence tying the resignation to an Iran-policy disagreement. The available linked report also does not identify who assumed the director’s duties or describe the transition arrangements. The distinction matters because a resignation during a conflict does not, by itself, establish that the conflict caused it. Gabbard’s reported departure can be recorded, but the political explanation in the populated summary should not be treated as verified. Independent evidence of an Iran dispute and the office’s transition details are still needed to explain the departure fully.
organization_tags: Office of the Director of National Intelligence

title: Korean Firm Paid Trump 2M While Affiliate Faces 105% Tariff
description_short: Korean Firm Paid Trump 2M While Affiliate Faces 105% Tariff
description_medium: Korean conglomerate Base Group paid 2 million to a Trump family business as nonrefundable development fee while Base Group aluminum affiliate faces 105.8% tariffs for circumventing Chinese aluminum duties. Democratic senators called the timing a particularly egregious example of Trump Administration corruption and potential bribery.
description_long: The supplied synopsis says South Korean company Base Group paid a $2 million nonrefundable development fee to a Trump family business while an aluminum affiliate faced a 105.8% tariff in a trade matter involving Chinese aluminum. It also attributes corruption and possible-bribery concerns to Democratic senators. I could not retrieve the linked New York Times article: the provided URL was rejected by the source reader, and a targeted search did not return the article. Without the report’s text, the record does not identify the fee recipient, the project or contract, the affiliate’s precise status in the trade proceeding, or which senators made the allegations. The timing described in the synopsis cannot establish that the payment influenced a tariff decision. Those details are necessary before the allegations can be explained or assessed, so this revision preserves them as unverified claims rather than presenting a causal connection as fact.

title: Babson Student Deported in Violation of Active Court Order Returns After Federal Judge Rules
description_short: Babson Student Deported in Violation of Active Court Order Returns After Federal Judge Rules
description_medium: Any Lucia Lopez Belloza was deported to Honduras despite a court order barring her removal. A federal judge later ordered the government to bring the Babson College student back within two weeks, after officials acknowledged the deportation was a mistake. The linked report does not confirm whether she returned.
description_long: Any Lucia Lopez Belloza, a 19-year-old Babson College student, was detained by immigration officers at Boston Logan Airport in November 2024 while traveling for Thanksgiving and deported to Honduras two days later. A federal court order had barred her removal while her case was pending. In February 2026, U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns ordered the government to bring her back within two weeks after the administration acknowledged that an officer had mistakenly deported her. The Associated Press reported that the judge acted after the government failed for months to resolve the error. The ruling addressed compliance with the court order and required her return; it did not settle her underlying immigration case. The linked article describes the order, but it does not establish whether Lopez Belloza actually returned by the deadline or what happened in her immigration proceedings afterward. Those outcomes remain unconfirmed here.
organization_tags: U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts

title: Justin Sun Buys $75M in Trump Crypto; SEC Fraud Case Halted
description_short: Justin Sun Buys $75M in Trump Crypto; SEC Fraud Case Halted
description_medium: The SEC and Justin Sun jointly asked a judge to pause the agency’s civil fraud case while considering a possible resolution. CNN reported Sun’s $75 million investment in Trump-family-backed World Liberty Financial and later described a proposed SEC settlement that would impose a $10 million penalty on Rainberry while dismissing claims against Sun and other defendants, subject to court approval.
description_long: The SEC and Justin Sun jointly asked a federal court in February 2025 to pause the agency’s civil case while they considered a possible resolution. CNN reported that the SEC had accused Sun and several companies in 2023 of selling unregistered securities and manipulating the price of Tronix; the allegations were not findings of liability. The same report said Sun had bought $75 million in World Liberty Financial tokens, advised the Trump-family-backed project, and that the family was entitled to 75% of token revenue under the company’s published terms. In March 2026, the SEC announced a proposed settlement: Rainberry would pay a $10 million civil penalty, while the remaining claims against it and all claims against Sun and two other defendants would be dismissed if the court approved the proposal. The record shows overlapping financial and enforcement matters, but the cited sources do not establish that Sun’s investment caused the pause or settlement.

preserved_fields.description_short: Justin Sun Buys $75M in Trump Crypto; SEC Fraud Case Halted

SEC’s March 2026 release describes a proposed $10 million Rainberry penalty and dismissals subject to court approval; these sources do not show the investment caused the enforcement outcome.

title: Trump Listed with 16 Phone Numbers in Epstein's Black Book
description_short: Trump Listed with 16 Phone Numbers in Epstein's Black Book
description_medium: A Vanity Fair article says Jeffrey Epstein’s contact book listed at least 16 telephone numbers beside Donald Trump’s name. The directory records contact information but does not establish how often the men communicated, what any number was used for, or whether the listing implies knowledge of Epstein’s crimes.
description_long: A 2021 Vanity Fair article reports that Jeffrey Epstein’s contact book contained at least 16 telephone numbers beside Donald Trump’s name. The article describes the book as a directory of Epstein’s social and professional contacts, compiled largely by Ghislaine Maxwell, and notes that it included people from politics, finance, royalty, and entertainment. It also recounts Trump’s public praise of Epstein in a 2002 New York magazine interview. The entry is evidence that the contact book listed multiple numbers associated with Trump; it does not show how often the men spoke, whether Trump personally used each number, or what any contact concerned. The article does not reproduce a complete underlying contact record, so the exact count and the classification of each number as personal, business, security, or property information cannot be independently checked from this source. A listing alone does not establish knowledge of or participation in Epstein’s crimes.

preserved_fields.description_short: Trump Listed with 16 Phone Numbers in Epstein's Black Book

title: Trump PAC Spends  Million in Donor Funds on Legal Defense
description_short: Trump PAC Spends  Million in Donor Funds on Legal Defense
description_medium: Federal election records revealed that Donald Trump Save America PAC spent over  million on legal fees in 2023, using donor money raised for political activities to fund his criminal defense. Donors were not informed their contributions would pay Trump attorneys. FEC complaints were filed over the arrangement. Trump various legal entities collectively spent hundreds of millions on lawyers across multiple criminal and civil cases, raising questions about whether his campaign was primarily a legal defense fund.
description_long: The linked BBC report, published September 23, 2022, cites federal election filings showing that Save America PAC paid more than $1.12 million in legal fees during 2022, including over $942,000 to Alina Habba’s firm for work connected to New York Attorney General Letitia James’s fraud case. The article also says another lawyer representing Trump’s adult children received nearly $185,000, and notes that the Republican National Committee had paid some legal bills. It describes a campaign-finance gray area and reports that experts saw no indication the payments violated a statute. This source does not support the title’s missing dollar figure or the supplied medium’s claim about spending in 2023; it covers different dates and does not document the specific FEC complaints described there. The amount, period, recipients, and complaint status for the 2023 allegation require the relevant FEC filing and complaint records before this entry can be completed.
